input.question: Why are our tongues more sensitive to spicy flavours rather than others?
input.ground_truth: "Spicy" isn't really a flavour in the same sense as bitter or sweet, it's an irritation. Salt, sugar and whatever activate taste buds on our tongue that create a sensation of flavour. Capsaicin (what gives things that spice) activates a sensor in our mouth that tricks the body into thinking it's burning. You're feeling a genuine pain from spicy foods, although no meaningful damage is occurring. Excessive spice will make your body react as though it were burning because that's the entire purpose of the receptors - to trigger the damage mitigation mechanisms your body has. A lot of salivation, opening the mouth, the desire to drink, sweating, the adrenaline rush and all that is what your body does trying to make the 'burning' stop.

Question: Why are our tongues more sensitive to spicy flavours rather than others?

Okay, imagine your tongue is like a special map on the inside of your mouth. On this map, there are little helpers called taste buds. Some of these helpers are really good at finding spicy things, like hot peppers!

When you eat something spicy, those special helpers on your tongue send a message to your brain that says, "Whoa! That's hot and spicy!" That's why you feel a tingling or burning feeling.

For other tastes, like sweet or salty, there are also helpers, but the spicy helpers are extra good at shouting, "Hey, I found something spicy!" That’s why your tongue notices spicy flavors more than some others.
